In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the white matter tracts of the human brain are not only important for the transfer of information between cortical and subcortical structures, but they also serve as a substrate for the modulation and integration of cognitive functions.3 The most prominent and consistent finding in white matter hyperintensity (WMH) is the association with age, with WMH increasing with age.4–7 However, the relationship between WMH and cognitive function is not well established.
the cholinergic system is not a single, homogeneous, and uniform system, but is composed of multiple, heterogeneous, and diverse systems.3
the cholinergic system is a diffuse one that is not limited to the basal forebrain but also includes the brainstem and the spinal cord.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cholinergic pathways of the basal fore brain in human are distributed in 4 major tracts: (1) the medial forebrain bundle (MFB), (2) the anterior commissure (AC), (3) the anterior internal capsule (AIC), and (4) the external capsule (EC).3–5
White matter lesions are common in elderly people.
the Ch4 pathway is more vulnerable than the Ch2 pathway, which is more vulnerable than Ch1, and Ch3 has the least vulnerability.
white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden in cholinergic pathways is a better predictor of cognitive impairment and Alzheimer disease than WMH burden in the whole white matter.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cholinergic fibers from Ch4 to the cerebral cortex and amyglala are located in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, while cholinergic fibers of Ch1, Ch2, and Ch3 are located in the genu of the corpus callosum.

white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden in these cholinergic pathways is a marker of vascular brain injury that may be related to neurodegeneration in Alzheimer disease (AD).3
In a recent study, we showed that WMH burden in cholinergic pathways was significantly associated with AD pathology in the brain.4 In the present study, we developed a novel visual scale to measure the extent of WMH burden in the cholinergic pathways in the brain.
